about: Where metrics come from. Every value in a metric's `mcp_patterns` must appear here, so a metric cannot claim a source that has no way of being read. Mirrored by hand rather than imported: CI for this catalog checks out this repository alone, so a source list living in the product would make the guard green here and wrong in CI.

sources.note: Google Search Console, pulled and cached by the platform. There is no analytics pattern behind it — the numbers are Google's, not Docsbook's own event stream, which is why its freshness and grain caveats differ from every other source here.

The goals and funnels DECLARED for the workspace, and what each one matches — not how they performed. Free on every plan: declaring measurement is not the paid part, reading the results is. Read it before judging any goal number, because a goal that matches nothing is indistinguishable from a goal nobody completes.

Completions per declared goal over the window, plus the daily series. Counted per VISIT, not per event — a section goal fires repeatedly for one reader, and counting events would report one person as five conversions. Served from the goal store rather than an analytics pattern.

Step-by-step completion of a funnel built from declared goals, with the worst TRANSITION named rather than the smallest step. Distinct from `forward_funnel`, which reads the single page route stored on the workspace: this one composes goals of any kind — sections, events and outbound clicks — so the route can end on a business outcome instead of a pageview.

Everyone who completed one goal, with time from first seen to converting, quoted as median and p90 and never as a mean — time-to-convert on a docs site is bimodal and the mean lands in the empty valley between the two modes. The source shown is LAST TOUCH and over-credits Direct; it is a hint, not attribution.

Visitors in the window with the goals each one completed. Read it, do not count it: a visitor is a hashed IP, so corporate NAT merges several readers into one row and a mobile network splits one across many.
